name: Pattani
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Sharma, D. D. 1989. Pattani (Manchadi). In: Tribal Languages of Himachal Pradesh, Part I (Studies in Tibeto-Himalayan Languages II), pp. 15-111. Delhi: Mittal Publications. Open scan: archive.org item CL-CSKHPKV-15657.
catalog_locator: sec. 2.8.3 'Accent', p. 35; sec. 2.5.6 'Tonalization', p. 31; sec. 2.8.2 'Length/quantity', pp. 34-35; sec. 1.4.1 'Quantitative variations', p. 22; sec. 3.1 'Syllabic Structure of a Word', p. 35; sec. 3.4 'Syllabic Division', p. 38; sec. 9.2.8 'Emphatic Particles', p. 104.
catalog_quote: 2.8.3. Accent: Pattani, like Dravidian, is a language with prominent accent on the initial syllable, but there are some instances of mono-syllabic words in which the stress, sometimes accompanied with high falling tone, becomes contrastive: /kà/ chest: /ka/ walnut; /si/ furrow: /si/ dead; /mè/ fire: /me/ without; /rè/ naval: /re/ eight. [p. 31, 2.5.6 Tonalization:] The glottal fricative /h/ tends to be realized as high falling tone in a prepausal position, as in /meh/ = /mè/, /goh/ = /gò/ hill, /ah/ = /à/ mouth, beak. In Pattani tone is, however, a non-phonemic feature.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: patt1248 (Pattani/Manchad, Lahaul; Sino-Tibetan) is not in the catalog. All three works with stress in the title are Glottolog mis-assignments: Yupho 1986 (two duplicate Glottolog records) and Hajek & Goedemans 2003 are about Pattani Malay (Austronesian, patt1249, southern Thailand); Glottolog's own reference pages say the link to Pattani [lae] is a 'computerized assignment from the term pattani' while the Zurich index gives Malay (Pattani) [mfa]. Yupho 1986 was downloaded open from the sealang Mon-Khmer Studies archive (scan without text; scanned at 200 dpi, one tesseract at a time) and confirms this: PM = Malay dialect of Pattani/Yala/Narathiwat; stress final by default, initial after an initial geminate. It is already the catalog's deciding source for patt1249, so it adds nothing there either; Hajek & Goedemans 2003 is paywalled (De Gruyter; Melbourne repository record has no public file). For patt1248 itself no item in this search of works with stress in the title is relevant; the best first-hand statement read is Sharma 1989 p. 35 sec. 2.8.3 ('prominent accent on the initial syllable', tone non-phonemic, a few contrastive monosyllables), already saved held by the project and re-verified against the PDF text; Grierson 1909 p. 454 explicitly has no information on Manchati accent. Priority acquisitions for patt1248 (outside the list of works with stress in the title): Sharma 1982 descriptive grammar (HathiTrust search-only) and Sharma 1977 'Syllabic structure of Pattani' (Indian Linguistics 38) — high. downloads by direct URL/API were used instead.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent falls on the first syllable of the word. Separately, a handful of monosyllables are distinguished by a stronger stress that may carry a high falling pitch (analysed by the author as the reflex of a final /h/, tone itself being non-phonemic).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress for Pattani (the same volume's Gahri chapter mentions secondary accent, but that is a different language).
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllabic minimal pairs where 'stress, sometimes accompanied with high falling tone' is contrastive (/kà/ chest vs /ka/ walnut, /sì/ furrow vs /si/ dead, /mè/ fire vs /me/ without, /rè/ navel vs /re/ eight); author treats the falling pitch as prepausal realization of /h/ and tone as non-phonemic. Vowel quantity: initial-syllable vowels short, final open-syllable vowels lengthened prepausally (1.4.1).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in the phonology ('Supra-segmental phonemes') section of a descriptive sketch based on the author's own fieldwork 1980-86 (informants from Pattan valley); citation forms. Utterance-level emphasis by 'heavy stress/pitch on the particular word' is treated separately (9.2.8). The statement is impressionistic, no acoustic evidence.
new_statements.identity_note: Sharma 1989 describes 'Pattani (Manchadi)' as spoken throughout the Pattan (Chandra-Bhaga) valley from Tandi to Udaipur, Lahaul; data from his own fieldwork 1980-86 with informants from the valley. This is Glottolog patt1248 (Manchad/Manchati/Pattani, ISO lae) at language level; no sub-dialect is singled out. Note the LSI-Himachal Pradesh 'Lahauli' chapter is Stod Bhoti (Tibetic), not this language, and 'Pattani' hits in our access caches (Hajek 2003, Pakkhem 2007) concern Pattani Malay (patt1249), not patt1248.

Accent: Pattani, like Dravidian, is a language with prominent accent on the initial syllable, but there are some instances of mono-syllabic words in which the stress, sometimes accompanied with high falling tone, becomes contrastive; /ka/ chest : /ka/ walnut; /si/ furrow : /si/ dead; /me/ fire : /me/ without; /re/ naval : /re/ eight.
new_statements.citation: Sharma, D. D. (1989). Tribal Languages of Himachal Pradesh, Part I (Studies in Tibeto-Himalayan Languages II). Delhi: Mittal. Chapter 'Pattani (Manchadi)', sec. 2.8.3 Accent, p. 35.
new_statements.locator: p. 35, sec. 2.8.3 'Accent' (p. 57); cf. sec. 2.5.6 'Tonalization' p. 31: 'Pattani tone is, however, a non-phonemic feature.'
new_statements.reading: Fixed word-initial stress (accent) in polysyllabic words; tone non-phonemic; the only reported contrast is a stress/high-falling-pitch distinction on a few monosyllabic minimal pairs, which does not affect placement. Under the catalog's scheme this reads as fixed initial stress (with a segmental/pitch prominence note for monosyllables). Independent confirmation is thin: Grierson 1909 LSI III.1 p. 454 (Manchati) states 'We have no information about the existence of tones and about the accent.' The fuller grammar, Sharma 1982 'A descriptive analysis of Pattani' (HathiTrust search-only) and Sharma 1977 'Syllabic structure of Pattani' (Indian Linguistics 38), were not obtainable; those remain the high-priority acquisitions for this language. Note the file was already held by the project from the earlier access pass (logged); this search of works with stress in the title re-read it against the PDF text.

tone_statements.citation: Saxena, Anju (1991). Tone in PaTani and Central Tibetan: parallel developments? and. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 14. pp. 129-136.
tone_statements.quote: PaTani has two distinctive tones: high and low. The following minimal pairs show that tone ts phonemic tn PaTani, The high tone ts represented here by “1” and the low tone is represented by “2”. ... PaTani has a word-tone pattern, where in polysyllabic morphemes only the first vowel has contrastive tone and subsequent syllable(s) have levelled tone, fe. If the first syllable has a high tone, then subsequent vowels have slightly lower pitch; and If the first syllable has a low tone, then subsequent vowels have slightly mid pitch.
tone_statements.locator: p. 130, sec. 2 'Tone in PaTani', /; cf. p. 133 'no falling tone' and p. 134 'the phonological word is the domain of tonal oppositions'
tone_statements.summary: Two contrastive tones, high and low, shown by minimal pairs; 'word-tone pattern': only a morpheme's first syllable contrasts, later syllables and suffixes take a levelled tone; no falling tone.

sources.note: Sec. 2.8.3 'Accent' (p. 35): Pattani has prominent accent on the initial syllable; in some monosyllables stress (sometimes with high falling tone) is contrastive (4 minimal pairs given). Sec. 2.5.6 (p. 31): /h/ realized as high falling tone prepausally, but tone is non-phonemic. Sec. 1.4.1: vowels short in initial syllables, longer in prepausal final open syllables. Sec. 3.4 (p. 38-39): syllable cut determined by 'accent (i.e. higher stress)' among other forces. 9.2.8: emphasis marked by heavy stress/pitch on a word (utterance level).
